questions.prompt: Why can a table have only one clustered index?
options: Because the clustered index defines the physical order of the rows, and rows can be stored in only one order
Because SQL Server limits each table to one index of any kind
Because a clustered index must be on the primary key, and there is only one
Because clustered indexes are stored in a separate file
questions.explanation: Creating a clustered index rearranges the actual data rows into the index order. Non-clustered indexes are separate structures, so a table can have many of them.

questions.prompt: For `SELECT Name, Salary FROM Employee WHERE Name = 'Aman'`, why is `CREATE INDEX IX_Employee_Name ON Employee(Name) INCLUDE (Salary)` a covering index?
options: Because it makes `Name` the clustered key
Because it forces the query to use the index with a hint
Because it contains every column the query needs, so there is no Key Lookup to the main table
Because it sorts the table by `Salary`
questions.explanation: `Name` is the key and `Salary` is included, so the plan shows an Index Seek with no Key Lookup. You run the query normally; there is no need to name the index.

questions.prompt: A table has 1 clustered index and 5 non-clustered indexes. How many structures does a single INSERT have to update?
questions.explanation: Every insert updates the clustered index and every non-clustered index, so more NC indexes mean slower writes.

questions.prompt: `Employee` has `EmployeeID` as the primary key, plus `UNIQUE` constraints on `SSN` and `Email`. What are `SSN` and `Email`?
options: Foreign keys
Alternate keys: candidate keys that weren't chosen as the primary key
Composite keys
Surrogate keys
questions.explanation: All three could identify a row, so they are candidate keys. Once `EmployeeID` is chosen as the PK, the other candidates are alternate keys, implemented with `UNIQUE` constraints.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson say to always index foreign key columns such as `Employee.DepartmentID`?
options: Without it the foreign key is not enforced
It turns the foreign key into a primary key
Parent DELETE checks, JOINs and cascades must search the child table, and the index makes that fast and reduces locking
SQL Server requires it before `ON DELETE CASCADE` can be used
questions.explanation: Deleting a parent or changing its key makes the database search the child table to verify the rule. On a large unindexed child table that becomes expensive.

questions.prompt: `Tickets.Status` has `DEFAULT 'Open'`. An INSERT supplies `NULL` explicitly for `Status`. What is stored?
options: `NULL`
`'Open'`
An empty string
The insert fails
questions.explanation: Defaults are applied only when the column is omitted or the `DEFAULT` keyword is used; an explicit NULL overrides the default.
